The wrong clue is given for exclave, it describes an enclave. 
Like Alaska, an exclave is a portion of a country separated from the main part by one or more foreign territories.
An enclave is, as the clue describes, a piece of land completely surrounded by another country such as San Marino.

I will never get why Americans seem to enjoy dad jokes so much. They are considered utter cringe over here, and those who engage publicly in groanery are near-universally derided, as it should be.

We call dad jokes "suchary" (literally, hardtack biscuits), and we describe them as "czerstwe", stale.

Karol Strasburger, a once-famous actor, became the host of the Polish version of Family Feud in the 1990s. (Interestingly, over here it is called "Familiada", which is a neologism based on "olimpiada", Olympic competition, that in no way indicates a feud - I have noticed over the decades that American versions of shows and game shows are usually more confrontational and filled with more engineered drama that their European counterparts). He always started the show with a suchar. "Nieśmieszny żart prowadzącego" (the host's uncanny joke) became a meme and entered our language as an idiom.

I have no idea when bad jokes became dad jokes but i ever so mildly resent it. 
Speaking as a father, I am just as unfunny or funny or punny or unpunny as anyone else. Indeed, if there is an age group that can be relied on to be painfully unfunny, it's children, with their repetitions of jokes and laughing at one's own joke or messing up the punch line. We love them for it, we get it, but let's not put fathers out there as some sort of class of people incapable of funniosity. 
Where are the mothers in all this? Delivering rock solid material that gets no one groaning? 
What this gets me thinking about, actually and away from the world's least furious rant, is a related rant: I ask you to consider whether  the generalizations about age groups, generations, regions, etc. to be a gateway drug toward worse biases. How long can a brain spend time saying trite stuff like "Gex X is so foolish," "Moms have no sense of fashion" or "Portland is full of weirdos" before being open to generalizations about identity, about gender, about ethnicity, religion, etc? 
I'm persuadable. Convince me that the lesser generalizations don't for some people open a pathway to worse.

As a retired ESL teacher, I can't stop myself from being THAT person:  Re your phrase"one of my wife's and mine idols."  

It's better to say "“One of my wife’s and my idols.”  Better still, "“One of the idols my wife and I admire.”

Before a noun, English uses possessive determiners such as my, your, his, and her. Here, both possessives modify idols.  Mine is a possessive pronoun and normally replaces the noun rather than modifying it, but should be used after the noun, not before.  You can say "That idol is mine", but not "mine idols".  Sorta picky, but that's the way English is.

I risk offending you or sounding like a language snob, but we come here to learn, right?

I think humans are coming to a reckoning that I think all "intelligent", competitive species face eventually (assuming there are other intelligent species).  And that is this:  how do we turn competition, which has been extremely beneficial for humans, into something other than tribalism, which is no longer beneficial to us?

Why is it that we simply cannot avoid an "us" vs "them"?

One answer is simple:  because there is so much media money to be made by making sets of people furious at each other:  different races, different genders, different life styles, different generations.  Nothing like a fight to bring in viewers.

There is a new documentary out that really has me thinking about this:  "Natchez" documents current life in Natchez, MS, a city where the "us" vs "them" is particularly visible, with the stately mansions and hoop dresses on one side, and slave markets (former, for now) on the other.

My Civil War historian son recommended it to me, and I heartily recommend it to others.

I’m not offended by the idea of “Dad joke”, though I am one (and one of the biggest offenders). That said, I would push back on concerted efforts to curtail humor and colloquial speech towards a PC goal, for want of a better term, or to avoid a slippery slope. I think it should be very obvious to any reasonable person that the idea of a “dad joke” just like “mom jeans” is good-natured and no one would take it seriously as a negative stereotype. Similarly, I can tell a “blonde joke” to my friends or my daughter in law, who is blonde, and they are well aware that I certainly don’t think most blondes are ditzy. I can even tell a Jewish joke to other Jews implying certain pecuniary tendencies with a good spirit, but of course a non-Jew telling the same joke in another context might be offensive.

All of this is to say, your concerns are noted and not without merit, but I personally wish our society was less prone to snap-judgments and rigid rules of offensiveness.

I think there are two ways to achieve groupiness  which I call cohesion and compression.
Cohesion: sharing a history, culture, experiences, and rejoicing and finding support in that sharing. Primarily generated internally and does not depend on denigration of otherness. Persists because of internal strength regardless of status in larger society.
Compression: forced by fear or violence to shelter together and support each other in the face of a common enemy. Primarily generated externally and depends largely on mutual denigration of otherness. Frequently dissipates when external pressures fade, leading to assimilation.
Sometimes compression and cohesion are symbiotic. 
Guess which I think is healthier? Guess where we are now?
